name: The Directors Behind the Masterpieces
description: Welles, Hitchcock, Kurosawa, Ray, Bergman, Spielberg and more: the filmmakers whose vision made certain movies feel like the work of one mind.

checkpoints.name: Studio masters
checkpoints.note: Charlie Chaplin writes, directs and scores his own films, and Modern Times (1936) is one of his best known. John Ford and Frank Capra make hit dramas and comedies for Hollywood, while Alfred Hitchcock builds a name in Britain before moving to the United States, and Billy Wilder begins his career in Europe.

checkpoints.name: After the war
checkpoints.note: Orson Welles makes Citizen Kane (1941) in his twenties, and Italian neorealism and Bicycle Thieves (1948) take cameras into the streets. Kurosawa's Rashomon and Seven Samurai, Ray's Pather Panchali, Bergman's The Seventh Seal and Hitchcock's Vertigo follow, and the French New Wave, under way from 1958, wins world attention with The 400 Blows (1959).

checkpoints.name: New waves and new Hollywood
checkpoints.note: Federico Fellini's La Dolce Vita and Hitchcock's Psycho both appear in 1960. The Battle of Algiers (1966) borrows the look of newsreel. New Hollywood brings The Godfather (1972), Jaws (1975) and Apocalypse Now (1979) from directors who learned from the world's cinemas.

checkpoints.name: Global screens
checkpoints.note: Steven Spielberg follows E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial (1982) with Schindler's List (1993). Pulp Fiction (1994) shows a new American style, In the Mood for Love and Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon (both 2000) bring Hong Kong and Taiwan sensibilities to wide audiences, and Parasite (2019) wins the Best Picture Oscar.
